units: fear has an identifiable trigger
fear stops once the danger is gone
anxiety points at a future and uncertain danger
anxiety shows up as muscle tension and damp hands
fear is compared to a brief alarm signal
anxiety is compared to a faulty, continuous alarm signal
both emotions start out with a protective function
telling the two states apart helps you respond appropriately
text: You are walking down a dark hallway when a door slams shut behind you. Your heart pounds, a chill travels down the back of your neck, your shoulders go rigid. That is fear. It has a precise cause, it arrives abruptly, and it subsides the moment the threat has receded. Anxiety operates on another principle entirely. Nothing definite ever stands before it; it looks ahead, toward whatever might happen. You feel it in a clenched jaw, in damp palms that stay damp for no reason you can point to. Fear is like an alarm that rings and then stops. Anxiety is like a badly wired alarm that hums underneath everything else. Both of them start out protecting you. What separates them is how long they last and what they are aimed at. Naming which of the two is traveling through you already sharpens the response you choose.

units: adults gather every week in a room used for stage practice
the workshop is aimed at people whom speaking in front of an audience blocks
the woman leading it previously worked in care
the session is divided into three categories of exercises
the first set of exercises works on breathing
the second set works on facial expressions
the third set consists of looking at each other in silence
this silent face-off often triggers a burst of laughter
the leader reads that laughter as a release
text: A handful of adults meet once a week in a studio whose wooden floor is scuffed and scratched. The workshop is meant for people paralyzed the moment they must address an audience. The woman who runs it worked in care before she turned to directing, and she builds every session around three families of exercises. The first set works the breath: draw the air in, hold it, release it in one prolonged sigh, until the throat finally loosens. The second set works the face: pull a grimace, hold it, drop it, and feel the gap between a tension you suffer and one you choose. The third set works the eyes: two participants stare at each other wordlessly, and one of them usually ends up laughing. That laugh is no failure, she says. It signals that a knot of awkwardness has just come undone.

units: the first step is to settle somewhere away from demands
you must rest your hands on your legs and breathe without forcing
the next step asks you to spot where the anger shows up physically
you are advised to name that area mentally
you then loosen the joints one by one
each release comes with a full breath
you must wait until the intensity drops on its own
the last step is to state briefly what you were trying to protect
that need is most often the need to be heard
text: Begin by sitting somewhere no one is asking anything of you. Lay your palms flat on your thighs, let the air sink to your belly, and do not try to push it along. Then look for the exact place where the anger has settled: a heat climbing into the cheeks, a tightness under the ribs, a stiffness in the fists. Name that place silently, the way you name the rooms of an unfamiliar house you are discovering. Loosen the joints one after another, the jaw, the neck, the fingers, granting each a complete breath. Wait for the surge to subside of its own accord; it always does, whatever route it takes. Then say aloud, quietly, the shortest sentence that describes what you were trying to defend. Often it was neither an insult to avenge nor a position to defend, merely a need to be heard.

units: volunteers were kept awake for a whole night
the study combines brain observation with measurement of sweating
the brain area in charge of detecting danger becomes more reactive
its reaction lasts longer than usual
the cause put forward is weakened control by the frontal area
frontal activity drops as the sleep deficit grows
participants perceive expressionless faces as threatening
they react sharply to low-intensity sounds
the resulting irritability damages the next night and restarts the loop
text: A research team has just released the measurements taken from volunteers who were held awake through an entire night. The protocol pairs brain imaging with continuous readings of the skin's conductance. Sleep deprivation reaches first the deep structure charged with appraising threat: it fires harder, and above all far longer, at perfectly ordinary images. The cause lies in the loosened grip of the frontal region, whose activity falls off as the sleep debt mounts. The consequence can be read directly in behavior. The volunteers take blank faces for hostile ones, flinch at barely audible sounds, and report clammy hands that linger well past the session. The authors close on a return effect: the irritability that builds up wrecks the following night, so that the cycle feeds itself.

units: the waiting area was set up in a cramped passage
the seats faced each other in two lines
a swing door produced unpredictable bangs
the ceiling lighting was dull
users left more tense than they arrived
the seats were regrouped into clusters turned toward the windows
a soft floor covering was installed to soften noise
a device was added to the door to prevent banging
the expected waiting time is now displayed
signs of irritation have decreased since
text: The waiting area of the department took up a narrow corridor, furnished with two rows of seats set face to face. Whoever sat there had nowhere to look but at a stranger, a swing door banged at unpredictable intervals, and the ceiling fixture cast a wan and colorless light over everything. Users came in tense and went out more tightly wound still. The care team therefore reworked the layout. The rows were broken into clusters angled toward the windows, a soft covering was laid over the floor to swallow the sound of footsteps, and the door was fitted with a damper. A wall panel now shows the expected wait, which lifts the most trying uncertainty of all. Since then the staff have reported a clear drop in gestures of irritation, and a calmer welcome for appointments that run late.

units: the text compares tracking by a digital tool with talking to a professional
the human exchange rests on a direct relationship
the professional notices cues the patient does not put into words
the digital tool captures neither shifts in the voice nor silences
the tool records assessments as data
the tool's strength is the reliability of its record keeping
human memory distorts and flattens recollections
the tool can reveal a pattern that went unnoticed
the author holds that the two approaches fill distinct roles
text: Should you hand your moods over to a digital journal? The question deserves better than the flat answers it tends to draw. A session with a practitioner rests on a living relationship: the voice wavers, a sigh escapes, and the listener catches what the account leaves out. Automated tracking hears neither the tremor of the voice nor the uneasy pause. It records ticked boxes and plotted curves. Its strength lies elsewhere, in a faithful memory, where recollection warps and flattens. A patient convinced he has been low for weeks opens the record and finds a pattern he had never noticed. The two devices, then, do not fill the same place. The journal measures and reminds; the conversation reads and accompanies. Setting one against the other means choosing between a scale and a gaze.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: she staffs a night-time telephone line
her post is in a room with no opening
she has held this job for many seasons
she names three qualities her role requires
the first is to bear the callers' silences
the second is to catch the audible signs of distress
the third is to detach once the shift is over
she walks home to shed what she has heard
a caller apologized for calling over a minor matter
she told him a minor matter deserved just as much attention
text: She takes calls on a crisis line late into the night, in a room without a window, and she has held the post for a good many seasons. Three qualities make the work, she says with a laugh. Patience comes first: she lets a silence stretch out, because a caller in tears needs someone who will not fill the emptiness for him. Then the ear: she catches a tremble in the voice, a breath held back, a sentence that breaks off at the same word every time. And distance last: when her shift is over she walks home and leaves behind what she has heard, or she would never get through the week. She recalls a caller, the other night, apologizing for troubling anyone over so small a matter. She answered that on this line, the smallest thing has the same right to be listened to as the worst.

units: the film begins with a long still image of an empty seat
this opening deliberately creates unease
the first part follows a family after a death
this part has neither narration nor added soundtrack
grief specialists speak in the middle part
the reviewer judges that these contributions weaken the film
the final part returns to the silence of the opening
the scene judged the most successful shows two relatives holding each other without speaking
the reviewer praises the absence of sentimentality
text: The film opens on a fixed shot of an empty chair, held long enough to leave the viewer uneasy. That opening choice announces everything that follows. The first stretch tracks a family through the weeks that follow a death, with no voice-over and no added score; you hear only household noise and, now and then, a stifled sob. The middle stretch shifts gear as grief specialists come in, and there the film loses its grip, because their explanations paper over what the faces had already said. The closing stretch returns to the silence of the beginning and delivers the truest scene of all, an awkward embrace between two relatives who cannot find their words. You leave the theater without any lift, and yet with the rare sense of having watched a sorrow handled without indulgence.

units: the writer explains to her addressee the reason for her long silence
she stopped replying after bad news
her withdrawal did not come from a lack of affection
every conversation forced her to go back over her pain
the isolation worsened her state more than the sadness itself
she has taken up walking in the evening again
the neighbors' questions still make her physically uncomfortable
she answers anyway and it is becoming easier
she invites her correspondent to get back in touch
text: I am writing because my silence over these past weeks must have hurt you, and you deserve to know where it came from. After the news you already know about, I stopped answering messages. It was not indifference. Every call required me to retell the story, and retelling it reopened the identical wound, so I went quiet, and that retreat cut me off far more surely than the grief itself. Here is what I understand now: the withdrawal, not the sorrow, is what made me so heavy to carry. I have started going out to walk again in the evenings. My face still burns when a neighbor stops to ask after me, but I answer, and each answer costs me a little less than the one before it. Write to me whenever you feel inclined. I promise nothing about cheerfulness. I do promise to answer the telephone.

units: a frequent question concerns whether slowed breathing really works
the explanation rests on a nerve linking the brain to the internal organs
lengthening the exhale activates that nerve
this activation lowers the heart rate
the protocols recommend a cycle longer than natural breathing
the exhale must last at least as long as the inhale
many patients give up after a failed first attempt
the initial failure is explained by breathing too deeply
you must reduce the volume taken in while stretching the cycle
it is advised to practice outside of tense situations
text: One question keeps coming back in consultations: does slowing the breath really settle anything, or is it a comforting belief? The mechanism is established. A drawn-out exhale stimulates the nerve that runs from the brainstem to the inner organs, and that stimulation brings the heart rate down. Second question: what pace? The accepted protocols stretch the cycle well past its spontaneous rhythm, giving the exhale a length at least equal to the inhale. Third question: what about failure? Many patients give up because a first attempt sharpens the alarm instead of easing it. The trouble comes from unintended overbreathing, brought on by pulling in far too much air. The fix is to shrink each breath while drawing it out, and to practice in calm before reaching for it under strain.
